newsitem.title: PERU: Peru warns of "emergency" as hostage health worsens.
newsitem.headline: Peru warns of "emergency" as hostage health worsens.

text.p: Peru warned on Monday that there may be health emergencies "at any moment" among the 72 hostages held in Lima by Marxist rebels in what has now become Latin America's longest embassy siege.

The mainly middle-aged and increasingly ailing captives have now spent 62 days under the guns of about 15 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels holding the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima since Dec. 17.
In Latin America's longest previous embassy siege, Colombia's M-19 rebels held 57 hostages for 61 days at the Dominican Embassy in Bogota before taking $2 million and a plane to Cuba.
Peruvian Health Minister Marino Costa Bauer said in a radio interview some of the hostages in Lima required permanent, close monitoring, for which a special medical team had been set up.

"It is possible that emergencies might happen at any moment," he said, singling out for special concern the cases of government legislator Gilberto Siura, former Supreme Court President Moises Pantoja "and two or three others."

Siura is being treated for cancer and Pantoja wrote to his family that he could hardly walk. "When I do, I lose my balance. My feet, hands and fingers have all gone hard. My arthritis stops me from reading and I can barely write," his message said.

The last two hostages released from the compound have been freed on medical grounds. Aid workers and police say the ailments of those left inside include hypertension, digestive problems, asthma and depression.

Japan's Asahi Shimbun newspaper said on Monday health conditions were deteriorating rapidly. It quoted a medic who visited the residence as saying: "We fear that if the incident drags on, inflammations and other diseases already present among the hostages will get worse and there may be a sudden outbreak of stomach ulcers or other stress-related conditions."
Despite three rounds of talks last week to set an agenda for negotiations between Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's government and the MRTA, there was no end in sight to the siege on Monday.

The day began with the now-familiar broadcast from the residence of an MRTA revolutionary hymn comemmorating fallen comrades. Half an hour later, police outside responded by blaring local "criollo" music -- with guitar rhythms and patriotic lyrics -- from loudspeakers aimed at the compound.

Last week's face-to-face talks at a Red Cross safe house between MRTA second-in-command Rolly Rojas and government negotiator Domingo Palermo raised hopes of a breakthrough after weeks without direct dialogue. But there has been no sign of a narrowing in two apparently intractable positions -- MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini's demand that 400 jailed comrades be freed and Fujimori's refusal to consider this.

"The liberation of our comrades is not negotiable," the MRTA's European-based spokesman, Isaac Velazco, told Peruvian television from Madrid late on Sunday. He referred to the hostages -- who include the brother of Fujimori, two cabinet ministers, the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats -- as "prisoners of war" and said the MRTA was respecting the Geneva Convention.
"Either there is an exchange of prisoners of war or there is no solution to this crisis," he said, adding that Fujimori could choose "a political solution ... or a military option."

There was no word on when negotiations would resume. Saturday's talks apparently produced nothing more than an agreement for mediators from the Vatican, Canada, the Red Cross and a Japanese observer to come up with proposals for "the continuation of the preliminary conversations."
